title: Soft Credit Inquiry: What It Is and Why It Matters
summary: Learn what a soft credit inquiry is, how it differs from a hard inquiry, and why fintechs use it (or skip credit checks entirely) for cash advances and BNPL.
body_markdown:
A soft pull is useful when you want to see whether an offer fits without creating a score event. A lender can inspect relevant credit-file attributes, then ask you to proceed with a formal application if you like the terms. That second step may create a hard inquiry, so “prequalified” doesn't always mean the entire process will remain soft.


### Where people get tripped up


The word “check” doesn't tell you which type of inquiry will occur. Apartment screening, insurance reviews, and financial apps can follow different processes, so ask directly before authorizing access. Look for wording such as “may result in a hard inquiry,” “will not affect your credit score,” or “no credit check.”


For BNPL shoppers, the same distinction matters. Some services may use credit information to evaluate an order, while others use different eligibility signals. Before using[Buy Now Pay Later tools](https://joingerald.com/buy-now-pay-later) , read the provider's disclosure instead of assuming every checkout works the same way.


A hard inquiry isn't automatically harmful, and a single application shouldn't stop you from seeking necessary credit. Still, knowing which consent you're giving helps you avoid an unwanted application-related pull when you only wanted an estimate or eligibility preview.


## Everyday Triggers for a Soft Credit Pull


Soft inquiries appear in ordinary situations because companies often need limited information before making a final decision. A card issuer might want to identify people who could fit a preapproved offer. An employer or property manager might need a permitted screening review. You might want to inspect your own credit history.


### Common reasons a soft pull appears


**Prequalification comes first for many lending journeys.** A credit card, personal-loan, or mortgage provider may review your file to estimate eligibility before asking you to submit a full application. The review helps you compare potential options while keeping the initial check score-neutral.


**Your current creditor may conduct an account review.** This isn't the same as applying for another account. The creditor already has a relationship with you and may review available information as part of managing that account.


**Employment screening can involve a soft inquiry.** An employer may request a credit-related report for a permitted, non-lending purpose, but that review isn't the same as evaluating you for a new debt product. The employer generally needs appropriate authorization and a valid purpose.


**Landlords and property managers may also check credit information.** Rental screening practices vary, so ask whether the review will be soft or hard before consenting. The same question applies to insurance underwriting, utility services, and telecom providers, since companies can structure their screening differently.


**Self-checks are soft inquiries.** When you inspect your own report through a bureau, monitoring service, or credit-score app, you're accessing your information for personal awareness. That activity doesn't count as an application for new credit.


**Some financial apps use a soft pull during identity or eligibility review.** A cash-advance or BNPL provider might want bureau information without creating a hard application event. Other apps don't connect to a bureau at all, which is a separate model rather than an especially gentle type of soft pull.


The key question is purpose. A soft inquiry gathers information for screening, monitoring, or prequalification. It doesn't represent a completed request for a lender to extend new credit.


## How Soft Inquiries Show Up on Your Report


Your own credit report can contain more inquiry detail than the report a lender receives. That's why you might see a soft credit inquiry that a lender doesn't see when reviewing your file for a credit application. The CFPB notes that soft reviews are shown to consumers when they inspect their own reports, while other lenders don't see those entries in the report version used for lending decisions.


Equifax and Experian state that soft inquiries can remain on a credit report for **up to two years** . Their presence creates a record of access for transparency and auditing, but the entry doesn't become a scoring factor because it remains listed.


### What to look for


Open the inquiry section of your report and read the description beside each company name. Soft entries may be labeled with terms such as “account review,” “promotional inquiry,” “consumer disclosure,” or “prescreen.” The exact wording can vary by bureau and provider.


A hard entry usually identifies a creditor and a credit application or account-opening purpose. If you don't recognize it, don't assume it's fraudulent immediately. First check recent applications, dealership submissions, lender marketplaces, and joint-account activity, then contact the listed company if the entry still doesn't make sense.
